implementation_notes: The metadata store is the attribute set on a plain struct: the derive macro reads field names and the sqlx(...) attributes (rename, rename_all, default, flatten, try_from, json) and generates an implementation of FromRow, the trait sqlx::query_as uses to materialise rows by calling Row::try_get per field. The reader is a procedural macro, so the mapping is compiled rather than interpreted, and a mismatch shows up as a decode or compile error in the generated implementation. When the schema itself should be the source of truth, Diesel's table! macro or SeaORM's entity generator are the alternatives.
pitfalls: Mapping is by field name unless renamed: a SELECT that aliases columns differently fails at run time with a decode error rather than at compile time.
Option<T> is the only null handling, so mapping a NOT NULL column to Option<T> compiles and quietly hides the schema's real constraint.
The generated implementation's bounds (Decode/Type per field type) produce error messages that point at the query rather than at the mapping declaration.

variants.name: Diesel table! macro + derived Queryable
variants.implementation_notes: Diesel moves the mapping into a compile-time macro: table! { users (id) { id -> BigInt, user_name -> Text } } declares the table and its column types as Rust items (the module it expands to contains the table struct, per-column types and all_columns), with #[sql_name = "..."] available for columns whose name is a Rust keyword, and derived traits on a struct bind its fields positionally to the column list of a query. Reader and engine are the macro expansion plus the query builder checked by the compiler, so a column referenced but not declared is a compile error - the strongest static guarantee among the Rust options - at the cost of keeping the declaration in step with migrations.
pitfalls: Field order in the struct is the mapping for a positional derive, so a Queryable over a column list in a different order silently assigns wrong values when the SQL types coincide.
The table! declaration duplicates the schema: a migration that is not reflected in the macro breaks the build (good), but a compatible-but-narrowed column type can coerce silently.

variants.name: SeaORM entities generated from the database
variants.implementation_notes: Here the metadata originates in the database: sea-orm-cli generate entity connects, reads the schema and writes entity files - a Model struct with #[sea_orm(table_name = "users")] and column_name attributes, the DeriveEntityModel derive, relation enums and ActiveModel - so the code generator is the metadata reader and the runtime traits are the engine. Queries are typed and CRUD comes from the generic entity layer. Choose it when the schema is the source of truth and an ORM-shaped API is wanted without hand-writing descriptors; note that generated files are ordinary source, so local edits are lost unless regenerated deliberately.
pitfalls: Generated entities drift from the database unless the generator is re-run; overwriting manual edits (or preserving them with generator options) is a maintenance decision either way.
Which tables exist in the mapping depends on generator flags and ignore patterns, so a skipped table simply has no entity to notice it by.
